prompt.en: A daytime forecast raises the LUF on a path from 4 MHz to 7 MHz while the MUF remains near 18 MHz. What should happen to a 3.7 MHz plan compared with a 14.2 MHz plan?

text.en: Both plans improve equally because LUF and MUF always rise together
The 3.7 MHz plan falls below the usable window, while 14.2 MHz remains inside it
The 14.2 MHz plan fails first because higher HF always has more D-region absorption
Neither plan can work because every usable frequency must equal the MUF

explanation.en: When the LUF rises to 7 MHz, 3.7 MHz is below the lower edge and is more likely to be absorbed or unusable. A 14.2 MHz signal is still between 7 and 18 MHz, so it remains a plausible path choice.

prompt.en: A forecast gives an afternoon MUF of 22 MHz for a path. If the operator uses an 85% OWF planning estimate, which target is closest?

text.en: 18.7 MHz, because it is slightly below the MUF
22.0 MHz, because OWF is exactly the MUF
11.0 MHz, because OWF is always half the MUF
25.9 MHz, because OWF is above the MUF

explanation.en: Multiplying 22 MHz by 0.85 gives 18.7 MHz. OWF is a practical choice below the MUF, not at or above it.

prompt.en: Which statement is NOT true when multipath is making a wide signal sound more distorted than a narrow signal on the same HF path?

text.en: Different path lengths can make components arrive with different phase relationships
Cancellation can vary across the occupied bandwidth instead of affecting every audio component equally
Using a wider signal prevents selective fading because all frequencies average together
A narrower signal may fit within a part of the channel that is less affected at that moment

explanation.en: Selective fading can be more noticeable across wider signals because different frequency components are affected differently. Making the occupied bandwidth wider does not remove the multipath phase differences.
